lead: Both readings turn the world’s values upside down in order to teach what lasts. James says that the lowly believer should boast in being raised up, and the rich in being brought low, because wealth passes like the flower of the grass. In Matthew, when a lawyer asks which commandment in the law is the greatest, Jesus answers with two: love God with all one’s heart, soul and mind, and love one’s neighbour as oneself. The two readings are close: what lasts is not what we own but whom we love.

set: James begins his letter with a section on trials (1:2–18), in which he says that tests produce endurance and that God gives wisdom generously to those who ask. In today’s verses he applies this to rich and poor in the community. The person of low standing is told to be proud of the high position God has given him, and the person of wealth to be proud of being brought low. Scholars discuss whether the “rich” here is a rich Christian, who is called to humility, or a rich outsider, as in 5:1–6. Either way, the logic is the same: wealth is not a lasting foundation.
The picture of the flower in the field comes from Isaiah 40:6–8 and Psalm 103:15–16, where human life is like grass that withers in the scorching wind, while the word of God stands for ever.
str: v. 9: the lowly believer should boast in being raised up.
v. 10: the rich in being brought low, because the rich will disappear like a flower in the field.
v. 11: the sun rises with scorching heat, the grass withers, the flower falls; so the rich wither in the midst of a busy life.
kw: In the Bible the word often means those who are poor and without power, whom God favours (Luke 1:52). It also means the humble in heart.
The same word as in 2 Corinthians 10:17. The only boast worth having is in what God gives, which includes dignity as his child.
vv: Let the believer who is lowly boast in being raised up, and the rich in being brought low
The ranks of the world are reversed in God’s eyes. The poor believer is raised by God’s adoption; the rich believer learns that wealth cannot save.
For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the field; its flower falls, and its beauty perishes.
A vivid picture of how quickly beauty and wealth fade. It teaches that our lasting treasure is not on earth.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God has a special love for the poor and that poverty of heart is a condition for entering the kingdom (CCC 2443–2446, 2544–2546). The Church’s teaching has always been that riches in themselves are not evil, but that attachment to them can close the heart to God and neighbour. The Second Vatican Council recalls that the Church is called to be a Church of the poor and to see in them the image of her poor and suffering Lord (Lumen Gentium 8).

set: Jesus is in the Temple in the last days before his Passion. After the Sadducees’ question about the resurrection (22:23–33), the Pharisees gather, and one of them, a lawyer, asks which commandment of the law is the greatest. The question was a real one among Jewish teachers, who counted 613 commandments and sought the principle that held them together. Matthew says the lawyer asked “to test him”, but in the parallel in Mark the scribe agrees warmly with Jesus’ answer (Mark 12:28–34).

Jesus answers from within the Jewish tradition, quoting two verses of the Torah: the Shema, “Hear, O Israel”, which every Jew recites (Deuteronomy 6:5), and Leviticus 19:18, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” His answer is not new in its parts; what is new is how he joins them and makes them the key to everything.
str: vv. 34–36: the Pharisees gather; a lawyer asks which commandment is greatest.
vv. 37–38: love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul and mind: the greatest and first.
v. 39: a second is like it: love your neighbour as yourself.
v. 40: on these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.
kw: A verb of committed, practical love that seeks the good of the other, not only a feeling.
The whole person: will and affections, life itself, and understanding. Deuteronomy has “heart, soul, might”; Matthew adds “mind”, perhaps for Greek readers.
As a door hangs on its hinges, the whole Law and the Prophets turn on these two commandments.
vv: Teacher, which commandment in the law is the greatest?
A real and long-debated question. Jesus does not set aside the other commandments but shows where they come from.
‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.’
Love of God asks everything. No part of the person is left out.
And a second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’
The second is “like” the first. Love of neighbour is how love of God is made real, as 1 John 4:20 says.
On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.
Everything in Scripture, from Genesis to Malachi, is explained by love.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Ten Commandments are summed up in the two commandments of love (CCC 2055, 2083, 2196), and that charity is the greatest of the virtues, the form of all the others (CCC 1822–1829). St Augustine’s famous saying, “Love, and do what you will”, is to be read in this light: if a person truly loves, what he does will be right (in substance, Homilies on the First Letter of John 7.8). The Church, honouring the Jewish roots of this teaching, remembers that the first commandment is the prayer that Jesus himself learned as a Jewish child, and that Christians and Jews share this heritage (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839).

study: James says that wealth is like the flower of the grass. What do I trust in more than God?
Jesus joins love of God and love of neighbour. Is there someone nearby whom I find it hard to love, and what small act of love can I do for that person this week?
